knowledge_point.title: Differentiating a Quotient Containing Other Functions

question.:question/problem:
If a curve $C$ is given by $y=\frac{2 \cdot 2^{x}}{x^{2} - 1}$, calculate the slope of the tangent line to the curve at the point where $x=0.$

The slope is {{field-1}}.
question.:question/worked-solution:
In this case, the expression for $y$ is a quotient $\frac{u(x)}{v(x)}$ with $u(x)=2 \cdot 2^{x}$ and $v(x)=x^{2} - 1.$

Therefore, we apply the quotient rule as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f^{\prime}(x)&=\frac{u^{\prime}(x)\cdot v(x)-u(x)\cdot v^{\prime}(x)}{[v(x)]^{2}}\\ &=\frac{(2 \cdot 2^{x})^{\prime}\cdot (x^{2} - 1)-(2 \cdot 2^{x})\cdot (x^{2} - 1)^{\prime}}{(x^{2} - 1)^{2}}\\ &=\frac{(2 \cdot 2^{x} \ln{\left(2 \right)})\cdot (x^{2} - 1)-(2 \cdot 2^{x})\cdot (2 x)}{(x^{2} - 1)^{2}}\\ &=\frac{2\cdot 2^x[(x^2-1)\ln 2-2x]}{(x^2-1)^2}\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope of the tangent line, we now substitute $x=0$ into the formula and get

$$
\begin{aligned}f^{\prime}(0)&=\frac{2\cdot 2^(0)[((0)^2-1)\ln 2-2(0)]}{((0)^2-1)^2}\\ &=\frac{- 2 \ln{\left(2 \right)}}{1}\\ &=- \ln{\left(4 \right)}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent line at $x=0$ is $- \ln{\left(4 \right)}.$
